![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14044310/assets/d84c6743bd4cc1ab3306951f507f4691ea3c3f2075ead5f04328f64254d5a786.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=-3$ and $x=0.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =x(x+3) \\ {y}^{′} & =x(x+1)(x+3) \\ {y}^{′} & =x(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can dismiss the equation ${y}^{′}=x(x+1)(x+3).$ Although the right-hand side evaluates to zero at $x=-3$ and $x=0,$ it also evaluates to zero when $x=-1,$ which is behavior not exhibited by our slope field.

- Second, the lines $x=-3$ and $x=0$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $x<-3$ | $-3<x<0$ | $x>0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Of the two remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=x(x+3).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=x(x+3).$
